Sep 24, 2026, 4:30 PM ET
Atlanta Braves star outfielder Ronald Acuna Jr. (shin) is starting in right field and is batting second against the visiting Cincinnati Reds and right-hander Brady Singer on Thursday, per MLB.com. Acuna fouled a ball off his left shin in Tuesday's game against the Reds and did not start on Wednesday, but he is back for the series finale and should be returned to all starting fantasy lineups against Singer. In just five career at-bats against Senger, Acuna is hitting .600 with a solo home run. The 28-year-old former MVP and five-time All-Star had two separate stints on the injured list this year with hamstring injuries, which has limited his overall production for fantasy managers. Acuna has hit .259 (102-for-394) with 20 home runs, 55 RBI, 20 stolen bases, and 60 runs scored. Braves fans can breathe a sigh of relief that they did not lose Acuna just before the start of the playoffs next week, and they will be hoping he can carry over his hot hitting in September. In 19 games during the month, he has gone 25-for-74 (.338) with seven homers and 19 RBI in 81 plate appearances.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com
More Recent News
Jesus Luzardo Throws Bullpen Session on Thursday


Keith Hernandez




Sep 24, 2026, 4:14 PM ET
Philadelphia Phillies left-hander Jesus Luzardo (shoulder) threw a bullpen session that consisted of around 30 pitches on Thursday, as expected, according to Matt Gelb of The Athletic. Luzardo said the session went well. The Phillies could look to have Luzardo throw a simulated game this weekend to face live hitters, and he remains very much in play to return to the starting rotation for the start of the postseason next week in the wild-card series. The Phillies must first get into the postseason, as they entered Thursday tied with the Chicago Cubs for the final wild-card spot in the National League, with the Arizona Diamondbacks on their tails at three games behind with four left to play. Luzardo will be eligible to come off the 15-day injured list for the regular-season finale on Sunday, but he almost certainly won't be an option to pitch in that game as the Phillies look to save him for the playoffs. Getting the 28-year-old southpaw back for next week is the team's top priority after he went 14-5 with a career-best 2.87 ERA, 1.08 WHIP, and 221:52 K:BB in 178 2/3 innings across 29 starts in his second year with the organization.--Keith Hernandez
Source: The Athletic - Matt Gelb
Sep 24, 2026, 4:08 PM ET
The Chicago White Sox announced on Thursday that they placed right-hander Luis Castillo (shoulder) on the 15-day injured list with a right-shoulder impingement and recalled right-hander Tyler Davis from Triple-A Charlotte in a corresponding move. The White Sox had recently sent Castillo to the bullpen, but he did not fare any better there, posting a 13.50 ERA in three relief appearances after recording a 7.52 ERA in his final six starts of the year. The 33-year-old veteran Dominican will finish his 2026 regular season with a 4-11 record, 5.85 ERA, 1.49 WHIP, 112 strikeouts, and 44 walks in 130 2/3 innings across 29 appearances (23 starts) with both the White Sox and Seattle Mariners. Castillo was much worse in his nine outings (six starts) with the White Sox, recording an 8.42 ERA, 1.81 WHIP, and 26:12 K:BB in 31 innings. He will be eligible to return for the American League Division Series in the playoffs, but we have most likely seen the last of Castillo with the White Sox this year.--Keith Hernandez
Source: Chicago White Sox
Alex Bregman Has Resumed Hitting


Keith Hernandez




Sep 24, 2026, 3:23 PM ET
Chicago Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman (face) did not return to the starting lineup for the team's series finale against the Miami Marlins at Wrigley Field on Thursday, but he has resumed hitting, according to The Athletic's Patrick Mooney. The All-Star third baseman continues to recover from a freak accident when he was hit by a foul ball while in the on-deck circle against the division-rival Cincinnati Reds on Sunday. Bregman suffered multiple facial fractures, but manager Craig Counsell has not ruled him out from returning for the final regular-season series of the year this weekend at Fenway Park against his old team, the Boston Red Sox. "But he's feeling good in terms of the hitting part. That went well. He's happy with how that went, so we'll just do a little more, run around a little bit more today and see how that makes him feel. And we'll just keep progressing," Counsell said. To be cleared to play this weekend in Boston, Bregman needs to get the swelling down around his left eye. Bregman is hoping that his strong month of September (.295 average, .968 OPS in 18 games) can shift seamlessly into the start of the postseason next week, despite his freak face injury last weekend.--Keith Hernandez
Source: The Athletic - Patrick Mooney
Sep 24, 2026, 3:16 PM ET
Miami Marlins infield prospect Jacob Lombard's first taste of professional baseball was a mixed bag while playing for Single-A Jupiter. The Marlins' fourth-ranked prospect hit four home runs, stole 11 bases, and registered a 13.1 percent walk rate in 22 games for the Hammerheads. He also propelled the team to the Florida State League playoffs (which they went on to win) by hitting a go-ahead home run with the team down to its final strike of the season, then went 5-for-14 (.357) with a pair of home runs during the playoffs. The downside was that he hit just .220 during the regular season, due largely to an astronomical 39.4 percent strikeout rate. If the 2026 first-round draft pick can make progress in that area next season, he should see time at High-A and perhaps even Double-A by season's end. At just 18 years old, it will be a few years before he debuts in the majors, but there is plenty of upside here to make him a worthy stash in dynasty leagues.--Jarod Rupp
Source: MiLB.com
Willson Contreras Won't Return in Series Finale


Keith Hernandez




Sep 24, 2026, 3:16 PM ET
Boston Red Sox first baseman Willson Contreras (hand) is missing a sixth straight game in Thursday's series finale against the visiting Cleveland Guardians, per MLB.com. Nick Sogard is making another start at first base and will bat out of the leadoff spot against Guardians right-hander Daniel Espino. Contreras was hit by a pitch on his right hand in last Thursday's game against the Texas Rangers. X-rays came back negative, but Boston has elected to give him some extra rest with the postseason starting next week. We would expect Contreras to return during this weekend's series at home against the Chicago Cubs. The four-time All-Star has hit a career-high 27 home runs while driving in 81 runs in 129 games across 533 plate appearances, but he has only played in four games in September after hitting only .217 (18-for-83) with three homers, 11 walks, and 26 strikeouts in 23 games in August. The Red Sox will need Contreras, who has been one of their most consistent hitters for the majority of the 2026 season, in top form if they want to make a deep playoff run.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com
Ceddanne Rafaela Back in Boston's Lineup


Keith Hernandez




Sep 24, 2026, 3:10 PM ET
Boston Red Sox outfielder Ceddanne Rafaela (hamstring) is starting in center field and batting sixth for Thursday's series finale against the visiting Cleveland Guardians and right-hander Daniel Espino, according to MLB.com. Rafaela returned from a stay on the injured list due to a quadriceps injury but was pulled on Wednesday night against the Guardians with tightness in his hamstring. An MRI exam on Thursday morning apparently ruled out anything concerning, and the power/speed threat and starting center fielder is back in action for the final game of the series at Fenway Park. It is great news for the Red Sox, who did not want to head into the start of the postseason next week without their starting center fielder. The 26-year-old will now have four games to try to set a new career-high mark in home runs, as he enters Thursday's action with 16 homers, 70 RBI, 17 stolen bases, 67 runs scored, and a .284/.319/.444 slash line in 536 at-bats this year. Rafaela was a first-time All-Star this year in his third full season in the big leagues.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com
Sep 24, 2026, 3:06 PM ET
Miami Marlins outfield prospect Cam Cannarella tore through the Miami farm system this season on his way to Triple-A, logging just 19 games at High-A, then only 34 at Double-A before earning the promotion to the minors' highest level. Although his strikeout rate spiked from 12.9 percent at the lower levels to 23.8 percent while at Jacksonville, the Marlins' sixth-ranked prospect maintained a strong walk rate of 14.1 percent and still hit .282 with an .813 OPS to go along with three home runs and 11 steals in 45 games with the Jumbo Shrimp. In all, he hit 15 home runs across all three levels, not bad for someone who doesn't have a highly rated power tool, so it's something to keep an eye on in 2027. If the 23-year-old can continue to produce home runs to go with his penchant for contact and a keen eye, not to mention his plus speed, there could be a valuable fantasy asset here who would be on the verge of making his MLB debut next year.--Jarod Rupp
Source: MiLB.com
Sep 24, 2026, 2:55 PM ET
Baltimore Orioles outfield prospect Ike Irish (knee) was enjoying his first full season of professional baseball earlier this year while playing for High-A Fredericksburg. The former first-round draft pick had really heated up before a torn left meniscus ended his season in late July. The Orioles' fifth-ranked prospect batted .361 with nine doubles, a triple, seven home runs, and nine steals over his final 26 games before the injury. The hot stretch pushed his season-long slash line to .286/.388/.528 with 16 home runs and 20 steals in just 76 games for the Keys. The left-handed hitter recently returned to the diamond and will head to the Arizona Fall League to make up for lost time. As such, he should be fully healthy come spring and looks ready to spend much of the 2027 season at Double-A. He likely won't make his major league debut until 2028, but the 22-year-old has shown good contact, plenty of power, and an ability to steal bases despite not having a ton of speed, so his dynasty arrow is pointing way up for the potential to impact multiple fantasy categories.--Jarod Rupp
Source: MiLB.com
Liam Doyle Finishes 2026 on a High Note


Jarod Rupp




Sep 24, 2026, 2:37 PM ET
St. Louis Cardinals pitching prospect Liam Doyle capped off his 2026 season with a strong start in the Double-A Texas League Championship on Wednesday, allowing just one run (zero earned) on four hits and two walks while striking out six batters in five innings of work. It followed his earlier playoff start in which the left-hander gave up just one earned run on no hits and five walks while striking out eight batters in only 3 2/3 innings pitched. The former fifth-overall draft pick spent the entirety of the 2026 regular season at Double-A Springfield, recording a 3.76 ERA, 1.31 WHIP, and a 17.6 percent K-BB% in 23 starts (130 K in 103 IP). His performance this year puts the Cards' top pitching prospect on track for Triple-A in 2027 and a possible MLB debut at some point next year. If there is one criticism, it is that his walk rate remained elevated throughout the season, coming in at 12.5 percent, but so long as the 6-foot-2 hurler can keep striking out batters at a high clip, then it shouldn't get in the way of moving up the ladder. The 22-year-old remains a strong dynasty stash.--Jarod Rupp
Source: MiLB.com
Sep 24, 2026, 2:29 PM ET
Colorado Rockies corner infield/outfield prospect Charlie Condon capped off a strong 2026 season by smacking a home run in his final game of the year. The Rockies' third-ranked prospect finished with 27 long balls in 130 games played, while batting .273 with a stellar .390 on-base percentage thanks to a 13.2 percent walk rate. The former third-overall draft pick continued to strike out at a high rate of 25.1 percent, though that isn't that out of the ordinary for a guy who has as much power as he does. The 6-foot-5 slugger surprisingly never got the call to the majors this year despite a few very hot stretches of production, but that doesn't mean he won't be in the mix for a roster spot in 2027. The 23-year-old has a shot to make the team out of camp next year, and even if he doesn't, expect him to be one of the first high-profile prospect names called up in 2027. The strikeouts could make him a batting-average risk for fantasy, but the pop he possesses will play well at Coors Field, and the right-handed hitter is still a solid dynasty investment.--Jarod Rupp
Source: MiLB.com
Sep 24, 2026, 2:11 PM ET
Tampa Bay Rays outfield prospect Theo Gillen recorded a strong 2026 season, one that began at High-A and finished at Double-A. The Rays' second-ranked prospect was promoted to Double-A after 57 games at High-A, and despite a dip in batting average from .342 to .288, he did not appear to be overmatched. The former first-rounder's strikeout rate actually improved there, from 23.8 percent to 19.8 percent, while his walk rate remained steady. All in all, the 6-foot-2 slugger slashed .315/.419/.546 with 22 home runs and 44 steals in 116 games and moved all the way up to No. 12 on MLB.com's top prospects list. His type of all-around skill set makes the left-handed hitter a valuable dynasty asset, and he'll have his sights set on Triple-A next year. Once he's knocking on the door to the major leagues, which could be as soon as later next season, even redraft managers should be keeping a close eye on him.--Jarod Rupp
Source: MiLB.com
Kevin Gausman Unsure When he Might Pitch Again


Keith Hernandez




Sep 24, 2026, 1:42 PM ET
Chicago Cubs veteran right-hander Kevin Gausman (shoulder) said his left shoulder is still sore from the diving play he made at third base in the loss to the Miami Marlins on Wednesday night at Wrigley Field, according to Bruce Levine of 670 The Score. Gausman is getting treatment, but he would not predict his availability to pitch in the wild-card series next week. The 35-year-old is now up in the air as an option to pitch for the Cubbies in Game 1 of the wild-card series next week against an undetermined opponent. In his final regular-season start of 2026 on Wednesday night, Gausman allowed two earned runs on six hits (one homer) while walking one and striking out seven in 5 2/3 innings in a no-decision. He had a 4.38 ERA and 1.29 WHIP in 23 starts with the Toronto Blue Jays to begin the year before being traded to the Cubs at the deadline in early August. Gausman was not quite as good in nine starts with Chicago, going 4-2 with a 4.83 ERA, 1.23 WHIP, and 57:11 K:BB in 50 1/3 innings pitched.--Keith Hernandez
Source: 670 The Score - Bruce Levine
Sandy Alcantara Will Not Start This Weekend


Keith Hernandez




Sep 24, 2026, 1:35 PM ET
Miami Marlins manager Clayton McCullough said on Thursday that right-hander Sandy Alcantara will not make one more start this weekend against the division-rival Atlanta Braves, according to Stephen Strom. However, Alcantara, who picked up another save in the win over the Chicago Cubs at Wrigley Field on Wednesday night, will continue to be available out of the bullpen. Alcantara is 100% healthy, but McCullough said he felt like it was the right time to give the right-hander a breather with the season coming to an end this weekend. Going into Thursday's series finale against Chicago, the 31-year-old Dominican has gone 13-11 on the year with a 3.89 ERA (4.09 FIP) and 1.23 WHIP with 152 strikeouts and 59 walks in a league-high and career-high 213 innings pitched across 35 appearances (33 starts). Although he will not make another start this week, Alcantara could still help fantasy managers vying for a championship if he continues to work as a high-leverage reliever in save situations with regular closer Pete Fairbanks (hand) done for the season.--Keith Hernandez
Source: Stephen Strom
Ceddanne Rafaela Undergoing MRI Exam on his Hamstring


Keith Hernandez




Sep 24, 2026, 1:27 PM ET
Boston Red Sox outfielder Ceddanne Rafaela (hamstring) is undergoing an MRI exam on Thursday on his injured right hamstring, manager Chad Tracy told Tim Healey of The Boston Globe. In his return from a quadriceps injury on Wednesday that had landed him on the injured list, Rafaela was pulled from the contest against the Cleveland Guardians with tightness in his right hamstring. The Red Sox are hoping it was just a cramping issue, but we will know for sure at some point on Thursday. Fantasy managers should not expect the starting center fielder to be back in action for Thursday's series finale against the Guardians at Fenway Park, but hopefully Rafaela will be ready to return for Friday's series opener against the visiting Chicago Cubs. The 26-year-old was a first-time All-Star in 2026 and is currently slashing a healthy .284/.319/.444 with a .763 OPS, 16 home runs, 70 RBI, 17 stolen bases, and 67 runs scored across his 136 games played. If Rafaela can return before the end of the weekend, he will have a chance to set a new career high in home runs.--Keith Hernandez
Source: The Boston Globe - Tim Healey
Xavier Edwards Remains Out of Marlins' Lineup


Keith Hernandez




Sep 24, 2026, 1:21 PM ET
Miami Marlins middle infielder Xavier Edwards (thumb) continues to sit for Thursday's series finale at Wrigley Field against the Chicago Cubs, per MLB.com. Jared Serna will make the start at the keystone for the Fish and will bat eighth against Cubs left-hander Matthew Boyd. The 27-year-old Edwards injured his thumb on Saturday against the San Diego Padres and has not played since. With the Marlins eliminated from postseason contention, they might elect to sit Edwards for the rest of the final week of the regular season. He has minimal power, but Edwards is a spark plug because of his speed and contact skills, and he is currently hitting .280/.360/.371 with a .730 OPS, a career-high six home runs, 52 RBI, 21 stolen bases, and 61 runs scored across 142 games played and 595 plate appearances in just his second full season in the majors. Edwards' next chance to return to the lineup will be in Friday's series opener in Miami against the division-rival Atlanta Braves.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com
Sep 24, 2026, 11:58 AM ET
Across 182 innings (31 starts) in 2026, Seattle Mariners starting pitcher Logan Gilbert has recorded a 12-11 record with a 3.81 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, and 197 strikeouts. While Gilbert has still been a very useful pitcher for fantasy managers, he hasn't been quite as dominant this season as he has been in his peak years. After posting a 32.3% strikeout rate in 2025, Gilbert's strikeout rate has fallen to 26.7% in 2026. The 29-year-old's numbers have taken a considerable hit lately, as he's posted a 6.65 ERA across 21 2/3 innings in September. Surrendering the long ball has been a major issue for Gilbert in the second half of the season. Across 56 1/3 innings (10 starts) since the beginning of August, Gilbert has allowed 14 home runs (2.20 HR/9). Heading into his final scheduled start of 2026 against the Los Angeles Angels on Sunday, fantasy managers may want to temper expectations for the usually dependable Gilbert.--Will Brady
Source: RotoBaller
Sep 24, 2026, 11:47 AM ET
Across 653 plate appearances in 2026, San Diego Padres outfielder Jackson Merrill is hitting .252/.300/.459 with 26 home runs, 86 RBI, 82 runs scored, and 26 stolen bases. The 23-year-old got off to a rough start to the year, hitting .219 with 10 home runs across 396 plate appearances before the All-Star break. However, Merrill has been red hot in the second half, hitting .300 with 16 homers across his last 261 trips to the plate. Merrill has been particularly key to San Diego's late-season surge as an offense, hitting .325 with four home runs, 16 RBI, 10 runs scored, and two stolen bases over his first 85 plate appearances in September. The star center fielder has lowered his strikeout rate this month to 18.8% while also posting elite barrel (19.7%) and hard-hit (62.1%) rates. Heading into San Diego's final weekend of the regular season, Merrill profiles as one of the top five-category producers in all of fantasy baseball.--Will Brady
Source: RotoBaller
Sep 24, 2026, 11:33 AM ET
Across 102 innings (19 starts) in 2026, Houston Astros right-hander Hunter Brown has recorded a 6-3 record with a 3.26 ERA, 1.27 WHIP, and 120 strikeouts. The 28-year-old got off to a rough start to the year, missing over two months with a shoulder injury and posting a 4.94 ERA across 27 1/3 innings in July. However, Brown has begun to rediscover his top form in recent outings. Across his last 33 1/3 innings (six starts), Brown is 3-0 with a 2.43 ERA, 1.20 WHIP, and 48 strikeouts. Brown has had issues with command all year long, and his 11.9% walk rate has led to an elevated WHIP. However, he's boosted his strikeout rate all the way up to 28.1% and has struck out 39.1% of the batters he's faced across his first four starts of September. Heading into his final start of the regular season on Saturday against the Athletics, Brown is beginning to look like the fantasy ace he was drafted to be ahead of 2026.--Will Brady
Source: RotoBaller
Sep 24, 2026, 11:21 AM ET
Across 501 plate appearances in 2026, Cleveland Guardians second baseman Travis Bazzana is hitting .245/.337/.404 with 15 home runs, 57 RBI, 53 runs scored, and 19 stolen bases. The 24-year-old's underlying batted-ball metrics are underwhelming, as he's logged just a 4.8% barrel rate and a 36.2% hard-hit rate. However, Bazzana's 11.2% walk rate is impressive for a young player and helps him get on base consistently and use his speed. Bazzana has also been red-hot of late, hitting .288 with six home runs, 15 RBI, and 11 runs scored across 69 plate appearances in September. If the former top prospect is starting to grow into his power, he could begin to emerge as one of the better second base options for fantasy managers. In leagues where he's on the waiver wire, Bazzana should be a priority target for fantasy managers.--Will Brady
Source: RotoBaller
Sep 24, 2026, 11:15 AM ET
Across 655 plate appearances in 2026, Minnesota Twins first baseman Josh Bell is hitting .255/.317/.416 with 20 home runs, 92 RBI, 76 runs scored, and two stolen bases. The 34-year-old may not have one clear standout skill, but he remains a steady source of power and run production. Bell has kept his strikeout rate manageable at 19.9% while still posting solid barrel (9.5%) and hard-hit (42.0%) rates. The veteran switch-hitter also remains locked into everyday playing time in the heart of the Twins lineup, putting him in a good position to rack up runs and RBI. item.content:encoded:
The Chicago Cubs already had enough to worry about heading into the final weekend of the regular season. Then Boston’s weather decided to join the playoff race.
The Cubs asked Major League Baseball for an additional roster spot ahead of their series against the Boston Red Sox, according to Bruce Levine of 670 The Score. MLB denied the request, leaving Chicago to deal with a crowded schedule using the roster it already has.
The problem is that the Cubs are not exactly looking at a relaxing weekend in Boston. A nor’easter is expected to bring heavy rain and strong winds to the area, forcing MLB to move Sunday’s game into Friday.
That means the Cubs and Red Sox will play a split doubleheader Friday, with games scheduled for 1:05 p.m. and 6:05 p.m. Suddenly, one baseball game became two before most people have finished thinking about the first one.
Why the Cubs wanted another roster spot
Chicago’s request was about protecting its pitching staff at a pretty important time.
A doubleheader can chew through pitchers quickly, especially when a team is already managing injuries. The Cubs wanted another player available to help absorb innings and keep their most important arms from being pushed too hard before the postseason.
Kevin Gausman also left Wednesday’s game with a shoulder issue, adding another concern to Chicago’s pitching situation. Justin Steele has been working in relief since returning from his elbow injury, so the Cubs do not have unlimited options behind their starters.
Then there is Alex Bregman, who remains out after suffering facial fractures when he was hit by a foul ball.
In other words, Chicago probably looked at its roster and the forecast and thought, “We could use one more guy.”
MLB’s answer was no.
Cubs cannot afford a weather headache
The schedule change matters because Chicago is fighting for its postseason position.
The Cubs entered Thursday one game behind the San Diego Padres in the NL Wild Card race, with the Philadelphia Phillies also close behind. Every game matters, which makes a doubleheader both an opportunity and a potential headache.
The Cubs also have to think beyond Boston. Their pitching staff needs to be as fresh as possible when October arrives, and another weather-related postponement could create an even bigger scheduling mess.
MLB has already looked at contingency options if the weather makes Fenway Park unplayable, including the possibility of moving a game elsewhere.
That is not exactly how Chicago planned to spend the final weekend of September.
The Cubs wanted one extra roster spot to make the weekend easier. They did not get it.
Now they have two games Friday, a nervous eye on the weather forecast and a playoff race that refuses to slow down. At least the Cubs can be thankful the nor’easter cannot throw a curveball.

When the Detroit Tigers signed Framber Valdez back in February, right before spring training started, they were hoping he was going to give them durability in the starting rotation behind ace Tarik Skubal. Unfortunately, things didn't go as planned in terms of wins and losses for the Tigers, who traded Skubal at the trade deadline to the Los Angeles Dodgers.
Valdez, however, has been as good as Detroit had hoped he would be in terms of durability this season. With Casey Mize was also traded at the deadline to the San Diego Padres, Valdez took over as the de facto ace for the rest of the season and maybe going into next season.
He made what could have been his final start of the 2026 season against the Washington Nationals at Comerica Park on Wednesday afternoon. After he threw his first pitch in the game, he joined some select company, despite lasting just 5.1 innings.
Tigers Pitcher Framber Valdez Joins Select Company
Valdez started well, retiring the first nine Nationals he faced before he ran into trouble in the sixth inning. However, Wednesday marked his 31st start of the season and according to the Detroit News' Chris McCosky, Valdez joined Kevin Gausman, Aaron Nola and Logan Gilbert as the only pitchers that have matched that number of starts in the same time span.
Against Washington on Wednesday, Valdez allowed four hits, two earned runs, walked three and struck out six before being lifted by Hinch. He faced 22 batters and threw 87 pitches. At this point in the season and with Detroit out of the postseason picture, there was no need to push him further on a cool day in the Motor City.
The 32-year-old Valdez had a lot of issues inside the Houston Astros clubhouse and with teammates on the field, but what can't be denied is his durability. The only season when Valdez failed to reach 31 starts was 2024, but he still made 28 starts and went 15-7 with a 2.91 ERA. Valdez finished seventh in the Cy Young voting that season, which was won by Skubal.
There are some big decisions facing the Tigers' front office this season and one of them will be how they are going to go about rebuilding their rotation. Sure, Skubal could come back, but that seems like a dream at this point. There is also the looming lockout this winter, which could create more delays in decisions, but building a rotation around Valdez is something that Detroit needs to do. One thing they can count on with the left-hander is durability, something that was on display this season.

Josh Naylor's walk-off single in 10th propels Mariners past Astros
(Photo credit: Joe Nicholson)
Josh Naylor lined a one-out single to center field with the bases loaded in the bottom of the 10th inning to score the deciding run as the Seattle Mariners kept their slim playoff hopes alive with a 6-5 victory against the visiting Houston Astros on Wednesday night.
Dominic Canzone drove in three runs for the Mariners (74-84), whose only chance to make the postseason is to finish in a three-way tie with Houston (78-80) and Texas (78-80), who are tied atop the American League West.
Yainer Diaz hit a tiebreaking triple in the top of the 10th inning after earlier hitting a two-run homer for the Astros.
Houston closer Josh Hader (4-2), who pitched the ninth, returned to the mound in the 10th to try and put the Astros into sole possession of the division lead. With J.P. Crawford the automatic runner, Hader walked Randy Arozarena before Canzone hit a slow roller to shortstop Nick Allen to advance both runners. A walk to Cal Raleigh loaded the bases and another to Julio Rodriguez forced in the tying run. Naylor lined the first pitch he saw from Hader up the middle to win it.
Mariners reliever Cooper Criswell (4-2) allowed one run on one hit with one strikeout in one inning.
The Astros opened the scoring with four runs in the top of the third off Mariners starter George Kirby. With one out, Allen doubled to left. Jose Altuve hit what turned out to be a single down the left-field line that deflected off third-base umpire Ryan Blakney's shin. Yordan Alvarez doubled to right, sending Altuve to third, before Isaac Paredes lifted a sacrifice fly to right. Diaz then lined a two-run shot over the left-field wall to make it 4-0.
The Mariners responded with three runs in the bottom of the inning against Astros starter Ethan Pecko. Lazaro Montes drew a leadoff walk and, an out later, Crawford grounded a single to right. Both runners advanced on a wild pitch. Arozarena walked to load the bases for Canzone, who lined a two-run single off the right-field wall. With two outs, Rodriguez lined a double to left to cut Houston's lead to 4-3.
The Mariners tied it in the fifth off reliever Josh Hendrickson, who was making his MLB debut. Arozarena lined a one-out single to center, stole second and scored on Canzone's single to center.
Pecko pitched 2 2/3 innings and gave up three runs on four hits. The rookie right-hander walked two and struck out two.
Kirby went five innings and allowed four runs on six hits. The right-hander walked three and fanned five.
--Field Level Media

Cubs RHP Kevin Gausman leaves start after injuring left shoulder
(Photo credit: Patrick Gorski)
Chicago Cubs right-hander Kevin Gausman exited his Wednesday start against the visiting Miami Marlins due to left shoulder injury sustained while making a diving tag in the sixth inning.
After the game, manager Craig Counsell told reporters that Gausman's non-throwing shoulder 'got extended weird, and it just grabbed on him a little bit.'
Gausman told reporters that he dislocated the same shoulder in high school.
'I hope I wake up and feel great tomorrow, but you never know,' said Gausman, 35, who added he would take something to 'get in front of it tonight.'
Gausman, whom the Cubs acquired from the Toronto Blue Jays last month, allowed a one-out, two-run home run to Kyle Stowers in the sixth to give the Marlins a 2-0 lead.
After Heriberto Hernandez walked, Miami's Griffin Conine hit a grounder to the right of second base. Shortstop Dansby Swanson fielded the ball and threw to first base too late to retire Conine. Hernandez tried for third, and Cubs first baseman Michael Busch fired to Gausman, who was scrambling to the bag. Gausman caught the ball at his feet and lunged to tag out Hernandez.
However, Gausman winced as he got up. Counsell replaced him with Javier Assad, who was warming up in the bullpen.
The Cubs, who need just one win or an Arizona Diamondbacks loss to clinch a National League wild-card spot, have been dealing with pitching injuries all season, with 10 pitchers making at least eight starts.
Gausman, who is 9-12 with a 4.51 ERA between the Blue Jays and Cubs in 32 starts this season, is 4-2 with a 4.83 ERA in nine starts for the Cubs.

Gausman struck out seven and allowed two runs, six hits and a walk in the first 5 2/3 innings. Miami’s Ryan Gusto allowed six hits and two walks while striking out five in 5 1/3 innings.
Chicago’s Pete Crow-Armstrong needed a stolen base to become the seventh player to join the 40-40 club but went 0 for 3 with a walk and remained at 45 home runs and 39 steals.

BALTIMORE – Somewhat fittingly for a team forced to make TBA a regular part of its starting rotation, Toronto Blue Jays ace Dylan Cease is finishing a Cy-Young calibre season in limbo after an MRI revealed inflammation but no structural damage to his right shoulder.
The 30-year-old, who’s struck out 239 in 169 innings while carrying a 2.40 ERA over 29 starts, said upon rejoining the team Monday that he and the club “are still drafting a plan” for his next steps, although he hasn’t been ruled out from starting again this year.
For him to pitch this weekend against the Cincinnati Reds, manager John Schneider said, Cease will need to be “feeling better with this time down and feeling like himself, and obviously the game meaning a lot” for the Blue Jays, who are nearing elimination in the wild-card race. If not, the first season of his $210-million, seven-year deal will have ended with a messy outing Friday in Texas where his career-low average fastball velocity of 93.6 m.p.h. was concerning enough for him to be sent out for imaging the day after.
“It’s good news, I'm not having surgery, there's nothing that's going to keep me out next year or anything like that,” said Cease. “It's just some inflammation of various kinds.”
Regardless, the disappointing way his season is ending is yet another blow for a Blue Jays rotation that lost Bowden Francis and Shane Bieber before spring training began, Trey Yesavage and Jose Berrios during camp, Cody Ponce 2.1 innings into his first start and Max Scherzer in late April, triggering an ongoing roster churn that had them opening the final week of the season with just two healthy starters.
Even after Yesavage’s activation from his second injured-list stint Monday to start against the Baltimore Orioles, the Blue Jays still had seven starters on the sidelines. A revolving door of arms made “trying to stay mentally positive about it” a challenge, said Schneider, while regular bullpen games meant extra strain on reliever workload not only on the day of, but the days before and the day after, too. There was so much up-and-down that three pitchers, Chad Dallas, also recalled Monday, Chase Lee and Lazaro Estrada, each were optioned the maximum five times allowed without needing to clear waivers.
All of that’s made sustained winning — a 15-14 May and a 17-11 August are their only winning months so far — especially difficult.
“I always say in order to win a few series in a row or to reel off seven or eight in a row, you've got to have a couple turns through the rotation that are pretty good,” said Schneider. “That's been hard to do this year.”
Throughout the season, Cease, along with Kevin Gausman until he was traded, held a threadbare staff together with elite innings every five days, helping to keep a struggling team afloat. But his velocity has been declining for a couple months and he first remembers his shoulder feeling “achy” before his July 25 one-hit, 120-pitch shutout at Boston.
Cease’s fastball averaged 95.8 m.p.h. that afternoon, his first time this season under 96, and hovered in that range through Sept. 2 before dropping to 94.9, 94.8, 93.6 in the three starts that followed.
“I've never really experienced this, it's always been pretty easy for me to throw hard effortlessly. I never really experienced max-effort throwing and it not coming out and all that,” said Cease. “But at the same time it still felt good to compete. And I feel like I've grown a lot as a pitcher in terms of using my pitch mix and executing and locating the fastball and stuff like that. It wasn't anything that was like end of the world. It was just kind of something that had to be dealt with and a part of trying to win is going out and taking the ball, no matter what.”
Trying to describe the feeling in his shoulder, Cease said, “I don't know if I would fully use the word painful, definitely a bit heavy and achy, just not normal,” and doesn’t believe it resulted from a single moment, but rather the wear and tear “of being a thrower.”
“I will say I think I learned a lot from this year in terms of going forward, how I maybe want to manage things a little better,” he said. “I've learned my body better from a season like this.”
Among the lessons he’s identified is the amount of throwing in-between bullpens he does and finding more opportunities to sneak in additional rest.
Bigger picture, the Blue Jays aim to search for some learnings as to why they’ve had so many pitching injuries this season. Other than playing in the World Series last year, there are no real through lines but they’ve already started looking.
“I think you look at each individual guy and what their workload was this year and what you can try to stay ahead of,” said Schneider. “I feel like we've done a fairly good job with that, with our relievers going back to spring training, trying to ease them in a little bit. And we'll have to look at that again with the number of appearances with some of these guys. We've already started to look at it and start thinking about throwing load in the off-season when it starts, how much rest is going to be needed before you do start and making sure that everyone comes in where they should be next year.”

The Cubs are as close to securing a trip back to the postseason as possible.
The North Siders need just a single win, or a single D-backs loss, over the regular season’s final week to clinch a spot in the NL Wild Card round.
Who will the Cubs play? And where will those games be played? Those questions won’t be answered until next weekend, most likely.
But with just six games remaining until playoff baseball, who will the Cubs need to step up in order to make a run at the World Series in a National League field filled with strong contenders such as the Brewers, Dodgers and Braves?
Here’s a look at who the Cubs need to do their part to get back to the Fall Classic for the first time since 2016:
Who will step up at the back end of the 'pen?
Who will close games? This is by far the Cubs’ biggest, and potentially most important, question that needs to be answered. Will it be Jacob Webb, who leads the team with nine saves, or will former closer Daniel Palencia, who just spun two scoreless innings in one of his most impressive outings of the year, be able to take that role? Manager Craig Counsell, who has used 14 pitchers to record saves this season, will be tasked with piecing together a bullpen that has limited experience in those situations.
The Cubs need Webb, who spun a scoreless outing in 24 straight appearances from June to August, to get back into form after allowing 11 runs over his past 7 2/3 innings (nine games). If Palencia, who has thrown 6 1/3 straight scoreless innings, can also replicate his success from 2025, it could be a major boost for a club that entered Cincinnati converting just four of its past 12 save opportunities.
Deadline acquisition Ryan Zeferjahn and lefty Ryan Rolison could also play a big factor late in games, but there’s also a secret weapon waiting out in the bullpen …
Can Cabrera be a reliable relief option?
That brings us to Edward Cabrera, who returned from a recurring blister injury on his pitching hand on Sept. 15 in a multi-inning relief role. That will be his job going forward as the Cubs hope shorter outings can not only keep him healthy, but potentially provide a small uptick in velocity. Cabrera’s first relief experience had mixed results (two runs in 2 1/3 IP), but he came out of the bullpen Sunday and tossed a scoreless inning on just nine pitches.
The best-case scenario of this temporary move to the bullpen? Cabrera turns into this year’s version of the Dodgers’ Roki Sasaki, which would immediately help stabilize the back end of the Cubs’ bullpen. Cabrera’s season hasn’t gone to plan, posting a 5.68 ERA in 15 starts between three stints on the injured list, but he still has a chance to make a significant impact when it matters most.
PCA still doing MVP things in October
Is it really fair to ask more of Pete Crow-Armstrong? After going yard again Sunday, the Cubs slugger is tied with Philadelphia’s Kyle Schwarber for the most home runs in the Major Leagues. He leads Chicago in batting average (.280), homers (45), RBIs (107), stolen bases (38), runs scored (118), on-base percentage (.371), hits (170), triple (eight) and games played (156). Got all that? Simply put, he’s put together one of the most impressive offensive seasons in Cubs history and he’s not done.
But he will need others to contribute in October. While run production starts with Crow-Armstrong, even if he performs to his NL MVP front-runner ability, he can’t do it all himself. The North Siders have to count on Seiya Suzuki, Dansby Swanson, Ian Happ, Alex Bregman and Michael Busch below him in the lineup to generate scoring chances.
Holmes stepping up as playoff ace
Clay Holmes and Matthew Boyd are the clear No. 1 and No. 2 options for the playoffs, but Counsell hasn’t yet revealed who will pitch in the all-important Game 1. Holmes had a strong August (1.55 ERA in five starts) in his return to the big leagues after missing nearly three months with a right fibula fracture, but he’s allowed 16 ER in just 15 1/3 IP across three starts in September (9.39 ERA).
That’s a worrying trend for a club with limited starting options in the postseason, but Shota Imanaga has stabilized recently after a down stretch in August, and veteran Kevin Gausman can provide multiple innings in whatever role the Cubs need during the postseason.

What, no italics? That's right, I'm abandoning the usual boilerplate intro for this final edition of the two-start pitcher rankings to issue a grave warning ...
Don't count on any of these guys actually making two starts.
They appear to be in line to -- and some indeed will -- but the second start would come on the final day of the season. With no tomorrow, a team can throw caution to the wind and pretty much use whomever it wants. I'm not saying it'll start someone on short rest, but a bullpen game or a spot starter? Why not?
And actually, I think the pitchers most in danger of losing their second start are the ones on the teams with a tomorrow -- i.e., the ones resetting their rotation for the playoffs. If they've already secured their spot prior to the final day of the season and one of their top hurlers is scheduled to go, they'll almost assuredly opt for someone else.
To reiterate, you should be skeptical of any pitcher listed here actually making two starts, but especially Zack Wheeler, Max Fried and Kevin Gausman. Maybe Cristian Javier, Nick Martinez and Robbie Ray as well. You're probably going to ask about Payton Tolle because you're likely to see two baseball indicators next to his name on your lineup page, signaling two starts, but I'm so confident he won't actually make that second start that I've left him out of these rankings altogether. Of course, you'll probably still want to use him with one start because he's that good.
That should the litmus test. If you wouldn't be comfortable getting just one start from any of these pitchers, you're better off not using him at all. item.content:encoded:
After going 0-for-10 with four strikeouts in the first two games of this series, Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong had himself another big day in the third contest. PCA singled, doubled, homered and stole a base and helped lead the Cubs to a 9-1 blowout of the Reds, a victory tempered by a freak injury to Alex Bregman. More on the latter anon, first let’s wrap this win.
The Cubs got on the board in the first inning. PCA led off the game with a single and stole second, his 38th [VIDEO].
The Cubs extended their lead in the third. PCA led off with a double. A note on that double from BCB’s JohnW53:
With his third-inning double, Pete Crow-Armstrong has at least 30 homers, doubles and steals.
Only one Cub had done that before: PCA, last year.
Forty players on other teams have done it, 12 of them also multiple times. PCA is among 10 with two. Alfonso Soriano did it four times; Barry Bonds and Jose Ramirez, three.
It was noted on the Marquee broadcast that PCA’s 40-HR, 30-double, 30-steal year is the first ever by a MLB center fielder — nope, not Willie Mays, not Ken Griffey Jr., no one, until now. I’ve said it before, but don’t ever forget what you are seeing from Pete this year — it is truly historic.
Anyway, PCA then went to third on a ground out by Seiya Suzuki. The Cubs then loaded the bases on walks drawn by Michael Busch and Bregman.
Per the Marquee broadcast, that’s 22 bases-loaded walks for the Cubs this year, the most in MLB.
With the bases still loaded, Michael Conforto struck out, but Pedro Ramirez followed with a two-run single to make it 5-0 [VIDEO].
Now to the Bregman incident in the fourth inning. With two out, Busch hit a foul ball that struck Bregman, who was in the on-deck circle, in the face. Bregman immediately left the game and was replaced by Matt Shaw. Here’s what that looked like [VIDEO].
Per Craig Counsell’s postgame remarks, the ball hit Bregman in the cheekbone, which is swollen. There was also a facial cut, but we don’t know anything beyond that. Hopefully it’s not too serious and Bregman doesn’t have a concussion.
While all this was going on, David Peterson was sailing along, striking out seven over the first four innings. The Reds made it 5-1 on a solo homer by JJ Bleday in the fourth.
The Cubs got that run right back in the fifth on a solo homer by Michael Conforto, his 15th [VIDEO].
If you’re keeping track:
Kyle Tucker, 16 HR, 515 AB
Michael Conforto, 15 HR, 294 AB
That blast tied PCA with Kyle Schwarber for the MLB lead. The Cubs also lead MLB in home runs with 217; as noted on the Marquee broadcast, the last time the Cubs led all of baseball in home runs was 1958, led by Ernie Banks with 47 in his first MVP season.
Peterson completed six innings, allowing three hits and just the one run on Bleday’s homer. Here are his seven strikeouts [VIDEO].
More on Peterson’s afternoon from BCB’s JohnW53:
David Peterson’s quality start was his fifth as a Cub, fourth most on the team. Shota Imanaga has 14, as many as the next two combined: Matthew Boyd, eight, and Colin Rea, six. Edward Cabrera and Jameson Taillon both have four. Five others have one to three.
Peterson could be a valuable weapon in the postseason, either as a starter or out of the bullpen.
The Cubs weren’t done homering, either. After Caleb Thielbar threw a scoreless seventh, Suzuki lofted his 25th into the batter’s eye to make it 9-1 [VIDEO].
More on recent Cubs home runs from John:
With their three home runs, the Cubs have hit nine in their last four games (three, one, two, three). They had hit 12 in their previous 14 games, since smacking a team-record nine at home vs. the Brewers on Aug. 31.
Edward Cabrera was given the eighth inning, a good low-leverage situation. He allowed a leadoff single and after retiring the next hitter, another Reds batter reached on an error by Ramirez. But Cabrera got Elly De La Cruz to hit into an inning-ending double play.
Colin Rea finished up with a 1-2-3 ninth, his first game action in 11 days, on just eight pitches. Here’s the final out [VIDEO].
The Cubs will clinch a postseason berth if the Yankees defeat the Diamondbacks Sunday, a game that’s just begun at the time of this recap. The Padres, tied with the Cubs for the top wild card spot with the Cubs holding the tiebreaker, are playing the Marlins in a contest in San Diego that’s also just underway. The Phillies defeated the Mets Sunday, so the Cubs still lead Philadelphia by a game. Thanks to the Mets for taking two of the four games from the Phillies over the weekend.
The Cubs have Monday off, then open the final regular season home series Tuesday evening against the Marlins at Wrigley Field. Kevin Gausman will start for the Cubs and Janson Junk will go for Miami. Game time Tuesday is 6:40 p.m. CT and TV coverage will be via Marquee Sports Network.

CINCINNATI — Veteran right-hander Kevin Gausman has been riding a roller coaster since joining the Cubs before the trade deadline. It’s not one he’s enjoying.
“It’s really frustrating,” Gausman told the Sun-Times, “especially after being really consistent for the last five, six years.”
Gausman has alternated good and bad outings for weeks, going from seven innings of scoreless ball to four innings with six runs, including three home runs. In eight starts for the Cubs, Gausman has a 5.04 ERA.
In his previous five seasons, one with the Giants and four with the Blue Jays, Gausman had a 3.34 ERA in 158 starts. With 2,083 innings on his arm in 14 regular seasons, he knows he’s dealing with wear and tear, and it isn’t easy.
“You’ve got to give yourself a little bit of grace when it comes to the workload that I had last year,” Guasman said. “My 13th year, I made it to the World Series. So for 12 years, I had one way of doing the offseason. I’ve been in a lot of postseasons but never made it very far.”
In his first 12 seasons, Gausman totaled 25 ⅔ innings in the postseason. Last year during the Jays’ run to the World Series, he totaled 30 ⅔. In 2024, a non-playoff year, Gausman began his offseason throwing regimen on Oct. 28, the same day as Game 3 of the World Series. In 2025, he started Games 2 and 6 of the World Series.
“So I threw for over a year, threw the most pitches in all of baseball, most starts in all of baseball, most innings,” Gausman said. “So with that and less time, it was tricky trying to figure out how I make sure that I’m ready for the start of this season while also giving myself a little bit of a break. I came to the realization that I just wasn’t going to have much of a break.”
He might be feeling that now. After all, Gausman’s season with the Jays wasn’t rosy, either. He had a 4.38 ERA in 23 starts. Knowing the load he carried last season, the Jays had him build back up slowly in spring training. But as Gausman said, there’s no manual to help a pitcher prepare for the season after a World Series run.
“It’s hard to tell whether it was last year or just a combination of my whole career,” he said.
Cubs manager Craig Counsell said another factor is at play: Gausman is basically a two-pitch pitcher, fastball and splitter.
“It puts a higher premium on his execution,” Counsell said. “The hitter’s got two pitches to think about. He’s paid for his mistakes a little bit more. But when you’re relying on those two pitches, that kind of makes sense.
“The split-finger is also more difficult to throw, but when you get it going, it’s really hard to hit. When it’s not going your way, you’re probably going to throw balls with it. And he’s two pitches, so there’s not another pitch to go to.”
Which begs the question: How will the Cubs use Gausman in the postseason? They acquired him with his postseason experience in mind, but he might not get a start in the wild-card series. He doesn’t know what his role will be in the playoffs.
“I don’t think anybody knows,” Gausman said. “Nobody knew Chris Bassit was going to throw [8 ⅔] innings out of the [Jays’] bullpen in the World Series and only give up one run. It’s going to take every single guy on this staff to do what we want to do, which is go to the World Series.
“It’s all hands on deck. I’ve pitched out of the bullpen in the postseason. If you’ve been starting all year, it’s different. But you’ve just got to go into it with the mentality that it’s going to take everybody, and if you tell them you’re fresh, the phone might ring and it might be you.”

The Toronto Blue Jays dropped their first game against the Texas Rangers. Their 7-1 loss dropped their MLB playoff chances to 14.8 percent. Meanwhile, the team announced personal news about George Springer.
Game 2 of their series against the Rangers is scheduled for 5:05 PM Mountain Time, 7:05 PM Eastern Time on Saturday, September 19th, 2026. Jose Soriano takes the mound for the Blue Jays as Cal Quantrill looks to squash their playoff hopes for good.
Toronto Blue Jays’ George Springer Personal News Emerges During Texas Rangers Series
Before the second game of their series against the Rangers, personal news about the Blue Jays’ Springer emerged.
His MLB profile page shows that Springer’s birthday is September 19th, along with a few other personal details:
- George Chelston Springer
- Nickname: Horhay
- Born: 9/19/1989 in New Britain, CT
- Draft: 2011, Houston Astros, Round: 1, Overall Pick: 11
As of today, Springer is 37 years old.
“A Special Day 4 Springer. Happy Birthday, Georgie,” the team announced on Saturday morning.
George Springer Was Recently Recognized For His Contributions Off The Field
Earlier this week, Springer was the Blue Jays nominee for the Roberto Clemente Award.
MLB.com states that “The Roberto Clemente Award is the annual recognition of a Major League player who best represents the game of baseball through extraordinary character, community involvement, philanthropy, and positive contributions, both on and off the field.”
Springer’s nomination reflects what he has done in the community this year and over the six years he has spent with Toronto.
The award has been around since 1971. It was first called the “Commissioner’s Award.” It was renamed the Roberto Clemente Award in 1973, after Clemente’s tragic passing in 1972.
George Springer’s Future With The Toronto Blue Jays
Springer is on an expiring contract.
The Blue Jays traded Daulton Varsho, Kevin Gausman, and Jeff Hoffman to the Houston Astros, Chicago Cubs, and Minnesota Twins, respectively, at the trade deadline. However, they kept Springer and Shane Bieber.
At the time, it was because keeping Springer gave them the best chance at winning. But will that hold true for next season?
With this season nearly over, and the Blue Jays playoff hopes all but gone, it’s time to take a serious look at if he has a future with the organization.
The Blue Jays are loaded with young talent, and should be leaning into that. This offseason, they might need to make the difficult decision of moving on from Springer, despite everything he has brought to the organization.
After all, Springer isn’t getting any younger.

The Dodgers continue to roll with a six-man rotation and will also be interested in setting up their rotation for the postseason, so with only six games on the schedule it’s highly unlikely that any of their starters are going to pitch twice. Yoshinobu Yamamoto will take the ball on Monday and it’s possible that he may get an inning or two on Sunday if someone else (Blake Snell maybe) gets skipped during the week, but he should be locked into lineups regardless of whether it’s one start or two, so there’s no actionable takeaways there.
The Brewers have also been utilizing a six-man rotation for most of the second half and with six games on their docket, it’s unlikely that any of their starters get a two-start week. Jacob Misiorowski is scheduled to start on Monday against the Phillies and it’s possible he could throw a few innings on Sunday as well if the Brewers want him to get the work in. He’s in all fantasy lineups no matter what though, so that wouldn’t change anything.
The Twins have been utilizing a six-man alignment as well down the stretch, so with six games on their schedule that means that everyone will just take the ball once. Bailey Ober is pitching on Monday and would be the beneficiary if any of their other starters were to get skipped during the week, but as of now that seems unlikely. He would make for a decent streaming option though with matchups against the Giants in San Francisco and against the Rangers at home.
The Mets are also rolling with a six-man rotation to end the season, so there are no two-start pitchers there either. Sean Manaea pitches on Tuesday (at Rangers) and could conceivably pitch on Sunday as well (at Nationals) if anyone gets skipped during the week. We’ll update here if anything happens to change.
Someone on the Yankees is likely to make two starts next week, we just aren’t sure whether it’ll be Gerrit Cole or Carlos Rodon. Both are scheduled to pitch in Tuesday’s doubleheader against the Rays and both would be on regular rest for the regular season finale against the Orioles on Sunday. It’s also possible that the Yankees mix in a bullpen game there and no one winds up with the two-start week. If we gain any clarity from Yankees’ skipper Aaron Boone over the weekend, we’ll update here.
Very similar to the Yankees’ situation, we don’t have a clear picture on what the Rays will do with their rotation next week. It looks like Nick Martinez and Drew Rasmussen are lined up for the two games of Tuesday’s doubleheader against the Yankees. One of them could end up pitching again on Sunday and give them a two-start week, but that’ll all depend on how the club plans to structure its rotation for the postseason. Rasmussen should be locked into lineups regardless and Martinez is still a decent option even if it’s just a single-start week.
The Blue Jays’ rotation is extremely short-handed at the moment, leading to much uncertainty on what they will do over the final week of the season. My best guess would be another bullpen day on Monday, and then if the team is still in the mix for a wild card on Sunday, you could see Max Scherzer draw a second start for the week. It’s a gamble for sure if you want to chance that he makes two starts, but it’s one that could wind up paying off.
The Nationals also plan to utilize a six-man rotation over the final week of the season, so none of their underwhelming options are going to wind up making two starts. Unless it was Cade Cavalli though, fantasy managers shouldn’t have interest anyways.
Going Twice…
Note: Probable pitchers as of September 18 and are subject to change.
American League
▶ Strong Plays
Logan Gilbert, Mariners, RHP (vs. Astros, vs. Angels)
While it has been a disappointing season overall for the Mariners in 2026, Gilbert has certainly done his job, posting a 3.69 ERA, 1.06 WHIP and a 194/46 K/BB ratio over 178 innings through his first 30 starts. That’s right in line with what expectations were for the right-hander coming into the season. He’ll look to finish the year strong with a pair of home matchups against familiar divisional foes that he has had all sorts of success against. In a week where the quality two-start options are quite limited, Gilbert represents one of the best overall plays on the board.
Drew Anderson, Tigers, RHP (vs. Nationals, vs. Pirates)
Drew Anderson has pitched very well since joining the Tigers’ rotation in early August, registering a 2.58 ERA, 1.28 WHIP and a 31/19 K/BB ratio over 38 1/3 innings. He draws a pair of really nice matchups to finish the season with both starts coming in the spacious confines of Comerica Park. I know that he’s hard to trust given the limited track record stateside, but Anderson actually makes for a very strong play this week and is someone that I’d start in all formats.
Jake Bennett, Red Sox, LHP (vs. Guardians, vs. Cubs)
Bennett has done a really nice job in his rookie campaign for the Red Sox, compiling a 3.78 ERA, 1.10 WHIP and a 90/20 K/BB ratio across 109 2/3 innings in his 19 starts. His performance has dropped off considerably in the second half though as he seems to be hitting a bit of a wall from a workload perspective. Since July 22 he holds a 5.14 ERA and a 1.32 WHIP over 56 frames. What has still been there is the strikeouts. He has punched out six or more batters in five of his last six starts. If you’re able to absorb the ratio risk and need to make up ground in strikeouts, he’s a strong option this week.
▶ Decent Plays
Cristian Javier, Astros, RHP (at Mariners, at Athletics)
As you can expect after such a long layoff, we have seen plenty of inconsistency in Javier’s performance this season. He appears to have shaken off the rust though and is rounding into form now. Over his last three starts, the 29-year-old hurler holds a 2.20 ERA, 0.98 WHIP and a 15/7 K/BB ratio over 16 1/3 innings of work. That’s enough for me to give him a shot in a two-start week against two familiar divisional foes. Having to pitch at Sutter Health Park to finish the week isn’t ideal, but the A’s offense is limping to the finish line and there aren’t any left-handed bats there that we should be worried about. I’d feel comfortable streaming him in all league sizes.
Daniel Lynch IV, Royals, LHP (vs. White Sox, vs. Guardians)
Lynch has struggled with the transition back to being a full-time starter after spending most of the season in the bullpen. In his first eight starts he holds an uninspiring 5.28 ERA and a 17/11 K/BB ratio over 30 2/3 innings. That’s not helpful at all for fantasy purposes. He has pitched better lately though, allowing just two runs over 10 innings in his last two starts while notching victories in both of them. He gets the opportunity to play spoiler against a pair of divisional rivals this week and the added intensity of those games should lead to quality results. I’d definitely be streaming him in 15-teamers and I may even take the plunge in 12’s if I needed another viable arm.
Shane Baz, Orioles, RHP (vs. Blue Jays, at Yankees)
Baz’s first season with the Orioles can definitely be characterized as a disappointment. He enters the final week of the season with an atrocious 6-15 record, 4.11 ERA and a 1.35 WHIP over 173 innings with just 152 strikeouts along the way. He has been way more hurtful than helpful for fantasy purposes. You should expect more of the same over his final two starts. He could give you 8-10 strikeouts with a chance at a victory, but it’ll likely come at the expense of a poor WHIP and an ERA that isn’t going to be helpful. If that still sounds appealing to you, go ahead and roll the dice.
MacKenzie Gore, Rangers, LHP (vs. Mets, at Twins)
Gore has had another extremely inconsistent season, leading to a disappointing 4.67 ERA, 1.3 WHIP and a 172/69 K/BB ratio over 165 2/3 innings in 32 starts. Even the strikeouts have disappeared lately, with just three in total over 11 innings in his last three starts. It’s possible that the dropoff in production has been due to the heavy workload, in which case, there’s no real reason to expect him to bounce back in a two-start week here. The matchups are good though and in some leagues the 6-8 strikeouts that he’s able to provide here could wind up being the difference at the end of the season.
▶ At Your Own Risk
Foster Griffin, Guardians, LHP (at Red Sox, at Royals)
While Griffin has been a breakout star in 2026 and one of the best waiver wire finds of the season, he has not been the same pitcher since joining the Guardians at the trade deadline and shouldn’t be blindly started in the final week of the season. Over eight starts since the trade he holds a miserable 5.79 ERA, 1.61 WHIP and a 35/15 K/BB ratio across 37 1/3 innings of work. It’s possible that he fixes whatever has been ailing him and gets back on track this week, but the more likely scenario is continued ratio damage. Perhaps the strikeouts and the shot at a victory are worth the trade off, but think twice before locking him into lineups this week.
Yusei Kikuchi, Angels, LHP (at Athletics, at Mariners)
Kikuchi has had a rough season overall, registering a 5.02 ERA and 1.55 WHIP across 57 1/3 innings through his first 12 starts sandwiched around a trip to the injured list. He has also notched just one victory on the year. His performance has been slightly improved since returning from the injured list and he’ll try to finish the season on a high note against two divisional foes. I’m not thrilled about the prospects of using him at Sutter Health Park in West Sacramento, as his long balls woes could lead to a disastrous outing there. I’d only start Kikuchi if I was desperate to make up ground in strikeouts and could afford the hit to my ratios.
Anthony Kay, White Sox, LHP (at Royals, vs. Rockies)
On the surface, a pair of matchups at the Royals and against the Rockies would normally make anyone a strong streaming candidate – especially in the final week of the season. There are some serious red flags to consider here though. Kay has really struggled down the stretch, with a 7.06 ERA over 21 2/3 innings in his last five starts. He also hasn’t completed five innings in any of those outings, and with there being a strong chance that the White Sox will need Sunday’s game to keep their playoff hopes alive, they won’t hesitate to go to the bullpen in that one either. He’s an extremely volatile play this week. He could wind up delivering eight strikeouts and a victory with solid ratios. He could wind up giving you six innings total with three strikeouts and awful ratios. It’s up to your risk tolerance whether you want to take the chance or not.
Brady Basso, Athletics, LHP (vs. Angels, vs. Astros)
Basso has been transitioning to the Athletics’ starting rotation down the stretch, but he has yet to work deeper than four innings in any game so far and is very unlikely to pitch deep enough to earn a victory in either of these starts. The overall results on the season have been mediocre at best and his limited strikeout ability isn’t attractive for streaming purposes. Unless your ratios can’t be impacted by poor performance and you’re desperate for a live body to try to pick up a couple of strikeouts, Basso is best left on the waiver wire.
National League
▶ Strong Plays
Jared Jones, Pirates, RHP (vs. Cardinals, at Tigers)
After shaking off a bit of rust in his return from the injured list, Jones has been terrific for the Pirates and for fantasy managers. Over his last 13 starts, he holds a 3.56 ERA, 1.10 WHIP and an 84/22 K/BB ratio over 65 2/3 innings – and that includes an eight-run debacle against the Mets. He has allowed three earned runs or fewer in each of those 12 other starts. He gets a nice draw for the final week and represents one of the stronger overall options on the board. He should be started in all leagues without question.
Zack Wheeler, Phillies, RHP (vs. Brewers, vs. Rays)
Wheeler is tentatively lined up to start twice next week, though if seeding for the Wild Card is already decided by Sunday, it’s very likely that he’ll get skipped or work in a very limited capacity as the Phillies structure their rotation how they want to for the postseason. That means it’s probable that he’ll only get a single start against the Brewers this week. He’s a strong option and should be started for fantasy leagues regardless, just be aware that he’s probably not going to end up making two starts.
Kevin Gausman, Cubs, RHP (vs. Marlins, at Red Sox)
The Cubs may wind up needing Sunday’s game for seeding purposes, but they’ll have already clinched a postseason berth and will want to align their rotation for the Wild Card series, so it’s possible that Gausman doesn’t wind up making that second start or is limited if he does. He’s still a quality option for the week as he starts off with a strong matchup at home against the Marlins and would be in most fantasy lineups regardless. Just understand that he may not end up making two starts.
▶ Decent Plays
Michael Soroka, Diamondbacks, RHP (at Rockies, at Padres)
If anyone is going to make two starts for the Diamondbacks in the final week of the season, it looks like it’s going to be Soroka. It’s not an easy draw though, as he has to battle the Rockies at Coors Field to start the week before finishing up with the Padres in San Diego. He has pitched well overall on the season and is coming off of a strong start against the Marlins his last time out. You can’t count on the ratios being as strong as they have been given the matchups, but the strikeouts and chances of earning a victory are still there. He makes for a solid streaming option in the season’s final week.
Robbie Ray, Padres, LHP (at Dodgers, vs. Diamondbacks)
As of now, Ray is lined up to make two starts next week, though his availability on Sunday will ultimately be determined by how the Padres choose to line up their rotation for the Wild Card series. Meaning he may end up with just a one-start week against the Dodgers in Los Angeles which is far from ideal. He’s probably still worth using, just understand that he probably doesn’t get two starts and his overall ceiling for the week is greatly diminished.
Andre Pallante, Cardinals, RHP (at Pirates, vs. Brewers)
To the shock and dismay of most fantasy prognosticators, Pallante has actually had himself a nice season in the Cardinals’ rotation, posting a 3.70 ERA, 1.26 WHIP and a 104/47 K/BB ratio over 151 innings while picking up 12 victories. He’s coming off of a brutal start against the Giants though where he was rocked for six runs on eight hits over his five frames. The matchup against the Pirates to start the week looks strong and he could be facing a Brewers’ squad missing most of its regulars on the final day of the season. As long as you keep your expectations in check, he’s a fine streaming option.
Janson Junk, Marlins, RHP (at Cubs, vs. Braves)
Junk has done a nice job logging innings for the Marlins this season, but he hasn’t been very helpful for fantasy purposes, registering a mediocre 4.50 ERA, 1.34 WHIP and a 78/31 K/BB ratio over 114 innings of work. He now has to finish the season battling two of the stronger offenses in the National League, which is most definitely not a recipe for success. He’s also not a big strikeout guy, so if you’re trying to climb in that category, there are probably better options on the board for the ratio hit you could take here. He has a higher floor than most doubles available on the waiver wire if you just need a handful of strikeouts and an outside shot at a win.
Blade Tidwell, Giants, RHP (vs. Twins, vs. Dodgers)
Tidwell has made 16 appearances (eight starts) for the Giants this season, logging a 4.56 ERA, 1.20 WHIP and a 42/21 K/BB ratio over 53 1/3 innings. What he has on his side this week is the strong likelihood that he’ll actually make two starts, and the second one against the Dodgers could come against a bunch of backups on the final day of the season. If you need seven strikeouts, decent ratios and an outside shot at a win, he’s probably worth a shot in deeper mixed and NL-only formats.
▶ At Your Own Risk
Andrew Abbott, Reds, LHP (at Braves, at Blue Jays)
Abbott has really struggled down the stretch for the Reds, compiling a 9.15 ERA over 19 2/3 innings in his last five starts. When he’s on his game, he is able to pile up strikeouts and is a threat to win, but he has not been in that form consistently in quite some time. The matchups are also tough, batting two potential playoff teams on the road. Once again, if your only concern is strikeouts and wins and you are alright taking on the ratio risk, you can fire away. If you care about your ratios at all though, I’d sit this one out.
JR Ritchie, Braves, RHP (vs. Reds, at Marlins)
With AJ Smith-Shawver getting moved back to the bullpen, it looks like JR Ritchie gets an opportunity to close out the season in the Braves’ rotation. His first start back did not go well, giving up six runs over 4 2/3 innings against the Cubs at Wrigley Field. The matchups are a bit better this week, but it’s not enough to trust him if you still have to protect your ratios. If all you’re trying to do is gain ground in wins and strikeouts and you need the volume, go ahead.
Mason Adams, Rockies, RHP (vs. Diamondbacks, at White Sox)
Never Rockies. There’s just no reason to do it, especially in a split week. Adams also hasn’t pitched well this season, posting a 5.09 ERA and 1.65 WHIP over 23 innings in his five starts. The only part that’s mildly appealing is the 23 punchouts. If you are unable to gain or lose ground in ratios and only care about moving up in strikeouts and wins (unlikely here), then you could look to him as a streaming option.
